approaches.title: Selection sort — place the next minimum
approaches.explanation: For every position, find the smallest value in the remaining suffix and swap it into place.

approaches.title: Bubble sort — early-exit adjacent swaps
approaches.explanation: Bubble the largest unsorted value to the end. Stop when an entire pass makes no swap.

approaches.title: Insertion sort — grow a sorted prefix
approaches.explanation: Insert each element into its correct place in the sorted prefix by shifting larger values right.

approaches.title: Top-down merge sort — divide and merge
approaches.explanation: Split until each range has one element, then merge two sorted halves with one temporary buffer.

approaches.title: Recursive bubble sort — bubble the max to the end
approaches.explanation: One pass bubbles the largest of a[0..n-1] to index n-1; then recurse on the first n-1 elements.

approaches.title: Recursive insertion sort — insert the last element
approaches.explanation: Sort the prefix of size n-1 recursively, then insert a[n-1] into its place by shifting larger elements right.

approaches.title: Quick sort — Lomuto partition
approaches.explanation: Partition around a pivot so smaller values move left and larger values move right, then sort both sides.

approaches.title: Single pass — track the running maximum
approaches.explanation: Every element is inspected once; keep only the largest value seen so far.

approaches.title: Single pass — maintain largest and second largest
approaches.explanation: Update the second largest only when a value falls strictly between the two tracked values.

approaches.title: One pass comparing neighbors
approaches.explanation: The array is sorted when no element is smaller than the one before it.

approaches.title: Two pointers — compact unique values
approaches.explanation: Because the array is sorted, write each new value immediately after the last distinct value.

approaches.title: Save the first, shift everything left
approaches.explanation: Stash arr[0], slide each element one slot left, then drop the stashed value at the end.

approaches.title: Reverse three times instead of shifting k times
approaches.explanation: Reverse the first k, reverse the rest, then reverse the whole array — the two blocks trade places in place.

approaches.title: Compact non-zeroes, fill the tail with zeros
approaches.explanation: Write every non-zero at the next free slot keeping order; whatever space remains becomes zero.

approaches.title: Check every element in order
approaches.explanation: No ordering guarantees, so the only option is to scan until the value shows up or the array ends.

approaches.title: Two pointers, skipping duplicates
approaches.explanation: Walk both sorted arrays together; matches advance both pointers and only new values get appended.

approaches.title: XOR of 1..n against the array
approaches.explanation: Every present number cancels itself between the two XOR runs, leaving exactly the missing value.

approaches.title: Reset the run on every zero
approaches.explanation: Keep a current streak of ones and the best seen so far; a zero resets the streak.

approaches.title: XOR everything — pairs cancel
approaches.explanation: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, so every duplicated number wipes itself out and the loner remains.

approaches.title: Sliding window over positive values
approaches.explanation: With only positives the sum grows as the window extends, so shrink from the left whenever it overshoots k.

approaches.title: Prefix sums with first-seen indices
approaches.explanation: Negatives break the window, so remember the earliest index of every prefix sum; a match k apart gives the best length.

approaches.title: Remember what the complement needs
approaches.explanation: Scan once keeping value → index; if the current complement was seen earlier, that pair is the answer.

approaches.title: Dutch national flag — three pointers
approaches.explanation: 0s grow at the front, 2s at the back; mid walks the unknown zone and swaps decide where each value lands.

approaches.title: Boyer-Moore voting
approaches.explanation: Keep a candidate and a balance; different values cancel the balance, and a majority survives every cancellation.

approaches.title: Kadane — extend or restart
approaches.explanation: At each index decide whether the best subarray ending here extends the previous one or starts fresh; keep the running maximum.

approaches.title: Kadane tracking the window boundaries
approaches.explanation: Whenever a fresh start beats extending, remember the new beginning; record start/end each time the best improves.

approaches.title: Track the cheapest price so far
approaches.explanation: Sell at today's price only against the minimum seen before today; the best of those trades is the answer.

approaches.title: Two write pointers, even for pos and odd for neg
approaches.explanation: Positives land at indexes 0, 2, 4... and negatives at 1, 3, 5..., preserving their relative order automatically.

approaches.title: Pivot, swap and reverse — the O(n) scan
approaches.explanation: Find the longest decreasing suffix; the element before it is the pivot. Swap the pivot with the smallest larger element in the suffix, then reverse the suffix to get the next permutation.

approaches.title: Suffix maximum sweep
approaches.explanation: Scan from the right, keeping the running maximum. An element is a leader when nothing to its right is larger.

approaches.title: Hash set with sequence-start detection
approaches.explanation: Put every number in a hash set and only start counting from sequence starts — numbers whose predecessor is absent.

approaches.title: First row and column as markers
approaches.explanation: Use the first row and column as markers for which lines must be zeroed, remember whether they themselves had a zero, then fix the markers last.

approaches.title: Transpose, then reverse each row
approaches.explanation: Transposing mirrors the matrix across the main diagonal; reversing every row afterwards completes an in-place 90 degree clockwise rotation.

approaches.title: Shrinking boundary simulation
approaches.explanation: Walk four shrinking boundaries — top row, right column, bottom row, left column — and close each side after it is consumed.

approaches.title: Prefix sums in a hash map
approaches.explanation: Keep a running prefix sum and a map of how often each sum was seen; a subarray ends in k whenever sum - k was seen before.

approaches.title: Nth row via the nCr recurrence
approaches.explanation: Build the row with the nCr recurrence: each value is the previous one times (row - col) over (col + 1), so no factorials are needed.

approaches.title: Extended Boyer-Moore — two candidates
approaches.explanation: Keep two candidates with two counters; a second pass verifies which of them actually appear more than n/3 times.

approaches.title: Sort, fix one, two-pointer the rest
approaches.explanation: Sort the array, fix one element, then run two pointers towards a zero sum — skipping duplicates at every level.

approaches.title: Two fixed loops plus two pointers
approaches.explanation: Sort, fix two indices with nested loops, then two-pointer the remaining pair to reach the target — long arithmetic guards the sums.

approaches.title: First index of each prefix sum
approaches.explanation: A zero-sum subarray lies between two equal prefix sums — store the earliest index of each sum and update the best gap.

approaches.title: Prefix XOR with a hash map
approaches.explanation: Keep the running prefix XOR in a map; a subarray ends in k whenever the current prefix and prefix XOR k were both seen.

approaches.title: Sort by start and extend the end
approaches.explanation: Sort by start time and merge into the last interval while it overlaps; a start beyond the current end opens a new interval.

approaches.title: Gap method — Shell sort style
approaches.explanation: Compare elements one gap apart across both arrays as if they were concatenated, halving the gap each round until it is one.

approaches.title: XOR split by the lowest set bit
approaches.explanation: XOR of all values with 1..n leaves missing XOR repeating; split every number by the lowest set bit to separate the two groups.

approaches.title: Merge sort that counts while merging
approaches.explanation: Every element taken from the right half during a merge forms inversions with all remaining elements of the left half.

approaches.title: Merge sort with a counting pass
approaches.explanation: Before each merge, count pairs with a monotone pointer — advance while arr[i] exceeds twice arr[j], then merge as usual.

approaches.title: Running maximum and minimum product
approaches.explanation: Track both the running maximum and minimum product, swapping them whenever a negative number flips the signs.

approaches.title: Linear scan
approaches.explanation: Check every element against x; return the index on the first match, otherwise -1.

approaches.title: Binary search — halve the sorted range
approaches.explanation: Compare the middle element with x and discard the half that cannot contain it.

approaches.title: Binary search on the answer
approaches.explanation: Lower bound = smallest index with a[idx] >= x. If a[mid] >= x it is a candidate, record it and move left; otherwise move right.

approaches.title: Binary search on the answer
approaches.explanation: Upper bound = smallest index with a[idx] > x. Only strictly greater middles are candidates, so move left on a[mid] > x.

approaches.title: Lower bound gives the slot
approaches.explanation: The insert position is exactly the lower bound of target — the first index whose value is >= target (or n if none).

approaches.title: Floor = ceil - 1 via one lower bound
approaches.explanation: The lower bound idx is the first element >= x, so it is the ceil; the floor is the element at idx - 1. Both are -1 when out of range.

approaches.title: Bucket positions by value
approaches.explanation: Store every occurrence index per value in buckets, then read the bucket of x. Linear but ignores the sorted order.

approaches.title: Lower bound + upper bound
approaches.explanation: First occurrence = lower bound of x; last = upper bound of x minus 1. Verify the bound actually points at x.

approaches.title: Frequency map
approaches.explanation: Count every value in a hash map and answer each query in O(1). Ignores the sorted structure.

approaches.title: upperBound(x) - lowerBound(x)
approaches.explanation: In a sorted array all copies of x form a contiguous block whose size equals upper bound minus lower bound. Repeat per query.

approaches.title: Binary search keeping one sorted half
approaches.explanation: At each middle, one of the two halves is sorted. If x lies inside that sorted half, search it; otherwise search the other half.

approaches.title: Sorted-half check with duplicate skipping
approaches.explanation: Same as rotated search I, but when a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi] we cannot tell which half is sorted, so shrink both ends by one.

approaches.title: Push toward the unsorted half
approaches.explanation: If the range is already sorted, a[lo] is the minimum. Otherwise the pivot lives in the unsorted half, so compare with a[hi] and move there.

approaches.title: Rotation count = index of the minimum
approaches.explanation: The array was rotated right by k, so the smallest element sits at index k. Binary search for it; a sorted range means k = 0.

approaches.title: XOR everything
approaches.explanation: Pairs cancel under XOR, so XOR of the whole array leaves the single element.

approaches.title: Binary search on the pair structure
approaches.explanation: Before the single element, pairs start at even indices. If mid is even (or odd with its partner on the left), the left side is intact, so go right; otherwise go left.

approaches.title: Linear scan for a local max
approaches.explanation: Return the first index whose value beats both neighbours (edges count as -infinity).

approaches.title: Climb the slope with binary search
approaches.explanation: If a[mid] < a[mid+1] a peak is guaranteed on the right; otherwise a peak exists at mid or on the left. Never need both neighbours.

approaches.title: Grow the root one step at a time
approaches.explanation: Keep adding 1 to i while i*i fits in n; the answer is i - 1.

approaches.title: Binary search on the answer
approaches.explanation: Search i in [1, n]; a mid is a candidate when mid*mid <= n, then push lo up to find the largest such i.

approaches.title: Binary search for the greatest i with i^n <= m
approaches.explanation: Search i in [1, m]; multiply i by itself n times (capping at m to avoid overflow) and keep the largest i whose power does not exceed m.

approaches.title: Binary search the speed k
approaches.explanation: Feasibility is monotone in k: if speed k finishes in h hours, so does any larger speed. For a candidate k the hours needed are sum of ceil(pile / k).

approaches.title: Binary search the day count
approaches.explanation: For a candidate day d, count bouquets made from windows of k adjacent bloomed roses (using an earliest-last-bloom running counter) and check against m.

approaches.title: Binary search the divisor
approaches.explanation: The divisibility sum is monotone decreasing in the divisor, so binary search the smallest d with sum of ceil(a/d) <= threshold.

approaches.title: Binary search the ship capacity
approaches.explanation: Capacity is monotone: greedy-loading days in order, a larger cap never needs more days. Lower bound = max weight, upper = total weight.

approaches.title: Walk the array decrementing k
approaches.explanation: Each present number a[i] <= k removes one candidate, so shrink k as you scan; the final k is the missing one.

approaches.title: Binary search on missing count
approaches.explanation: a[i] - (i + 1) numbers are missing up to index i and this count is non-decreasing, so binary search the first index with at least k missing and derive the answer from there.

approaches.title: Binary search the largest minimum distance
approaches.explanation: Greedily place cows keeping at least d apart; feasibility is monotone in d, so binary search the maximum d that fits c cows.

approaches.title: Binary search the maximum pages per student
approaches.explanation: Assign books in order to at most m students without any student exceeding the cap; the cap is monotone, so binary search the smallest feasible cap.

approaches.title: Binary search the largest subarray sum
approaches.explanation: Same monotone split as book allocation: greedy count of subarrays with sum <= cap; find the smallest cap allowing k subarrays.

approaches.title: Binary search the maximum board units per painter
approaches.explanation: Painter's partition is identical to book allocation: binary search the smallest per-painter cap that lets k painters finish all boards in order.

approaches.title: Binary search the real max distance
approaches.explanation: For a real candidate d, a gap needs ceil(gap/d)-1 extra stations. Binary search d on [0, maxGap] to 1e-6 and take the smallest feasible d.

approaches.title: Merge counting to the median index
approaches.explanation: Two-pointer merge until reaching the middle index; keeps both halves of the merged order without building the array.

approaches.title: Binary search the partition
approaches.explanation: Cut the smaller array at i and derive j so the left half has the right size; binary search i until maxLeft <= minRight across both arrays.

approaches.title: Merge to the k-th element
approaches.explanation: Two-pointer merge, consuming the smaller head until k elements have been emitted.

approaches.title: Discard k/2 elements each round
approaches.explanation: Compare the k/2-th remaining element of each array and discard the smaller block, since it cannot contain the k-th element.

approaches.title: Lower bound of 1 in each row
approaches.explanation: Rows are sorted with 1s first, so the count of 1s is n - lowerBound(1). Track the row with the maximum.

approaches.title: Binary search over the flattened index
approaches.explanation: Treat the matrix as one sorted array of length m*n; map a virtual mid back to (mid/n, mid%n).

approaches.title: Staircase walk from top-right
approaches.explanation: Rows and columns ascend. Start top-right: move left if the value is too big, down if too small — each step eliminates a row or column.

approaches.title: Binary search on columns with row scan
approaches.explanation: Pick the middle column, take its row-maximum; if that cell beats its horizontal neighbours it is a peak, else recurse toward the larger side.

approaches.title: Binary search the value by count <= mid
approaches.explanation: Rows are sorted, so count elements <= a candidate value via upper bound per row. The median is the smallest value with count >= (m*n+1)/2.

approaches.title: Track primitive groups by depth
approaches.explanation: Maintain a balance counter; a '(' at balance 0 opens a primitive. Emit only parens that sit at depth >= 1, then strip the outer pair of each primitive.

approaches.title: Reverse the list of words
approaches.explanation: Split on runs of spaces into words, then join them back in reverse order with single spaces.

approaches.title: Palindrome check — two pointers
approaches.explanation: Compare characters from both ends moving inward; a mismatch means it is not a palindrome.

approaches.title: Rightmost odd digit ends the answer
approaches.explanation: A number is odd iff its last digit is odd. Find the rightmost odd digit; the prefix up to and including it is the largest odd substring.

approaches.title: Compare column by column
approaches.explanation: Walk index by index, comparing every string's character at that position to the first string's; stop at the first mismatch or shortest end.

approaches.title: Two bijection maps
approaches.explanation: Map s->t and t->s consistently; any conflicting mapping means the strings are not isomorphic.

approaches.title: Rotation test via s + s
approaches.explanation: goal is a rotation of s iff lengths match and the doubled string s+s contains goal as a substring.

approaches.title: Sort and compare
approaches.explanation: Anagrams are equal after sorting both strings.

approaches.title: Single frequency array
approaches.explanation: Increment counts for s and decrement for t over a 26-letter array; a non-zero count means not an anagram.

approaches.title: Bucket by frequency, then sort
approaches.explanation: Count each character, then emit characters ordered by decreasing frequency (ties broken arbitrarily).

approaches.title: Running depth = balance
approaches.explanation: Track the current nesting depth via a balance counter; the maximum depth reached is the answer.

approaches.title: Subtract when a smaller value precedes
approaches.explanation: Read values left to right; if a symbol is smaller than the one after it (like IV) subtract it, otherwise add it.

approaches.title: Skip spaces, sign, then clamp digits
approaches.explanation: Trim leading spaces, read an optional sign, accumulate digits and clamp to the 32-bit INT_MAX/INT_MIN range on overflow.

approaches.title: Count via last seen of each character
approaches.explanation: For substrings needing at least one of '0','1','2': at each end index, the number of valid starts equals 1 + min(last-positions of the three). Sum over all ends.

approaches.title: Expand around every center
approaches.explanation: Try all 2n-1 odd and even centers, expanding while the mirrored characters match; keep the longest span.

approaches.title: Frequency array per substring
approaches.explanation: For every start, extend the end and maintain a 26-count array; beauty = maxFreq - minFreq (over present letters). Accumulate.

approaches.title: Reverse characters inside each word
approaches.explanation: Split into words and reverse the characters of each word in place, keeping the words in their original order.

approaches.title: Point the new node at the old head
approaches.explanation: Create the node, link its next to the current head, and return it as the new head.

approaches.title: Return the second node
approaches.explanation: The new head is simply head.next; guard against an empty list.

approaches.title: Walk and count nodes
approaches.explanation: Traverse next pointers until null, incrementing a counter.

approaches.title: Linear search for the key
approaches.explanation: Compare each node's value to key; return true on the first match.

approaches.title: Insert before the DLL head
approaches.explanation: Link the new node's next to the old head, fix the old head's prev, and return the new head.

approaches.title: Advance the DLL head
approaches.explanation: Move to head.next and clear its prev pointer so it becomes the new head.

approaches.title: Swap prev/next on every node
approaches.explanation: For each node exchange its prev and next links; the reversed list's head is the last node visited.

approaches.title: Slow/fast pointers
approaches.explanation: Advance fast two steps and slow one; when fast hits the end, slow is at the middle.

approaches.title: Iterative three-pointer reverse
approaches.explanation: Walk prev/curr/next, re-pointing curr.next to prev as you advance.

approaches.title: Recursive reverse
approaches.explanation: Recurse to the tail, then on unwind make the next node point back to the current one and cut the forward link.

approaches.title: Visited-node set
approaches.explanation: Store seen node references; revisiting one proves a loop.

approaches.title: Floyd cycle detection
approaches.explanation: If the slow and fast pointers ever meet, a cycle exists; if fast reaches null there is none.

approaches.title: Floyd then reset to the entry
approaches.explanation: After meeting inside the loop, move one pointer back to head and advance both one step; they meet at the loop's start.

approaches.title: Count nodes around the cycle
approaches.explanation: Once slow and fast meet, keep walking fast until it returns to the meeting point, counting the loop length.

approaches.title: Reverse the second half and compare
approaches.explanation: Find the middle, reverse the back half, then compare it node-by-node with the front half.

approaches.title: Split into odd/even chains then join
approaches.explanation: Build one list of odd-valued nodes and one of even-valued nodes, then concatenate them.

approaches.title: Lead pointer n ahead
approaches.explanation: Advance a fast pointer n+1 steps past a dummy head, then move both until fast ends; slow.next is the node to remove.

approaches.title: Find the node before the middle
approaches.explanation: Use a slow/fast pair with a prev tracker; when fast finishes, prev precedes the middle, so skip it.

approaches.title: Merge sort on the list
approaches.explanation: Split at the middle with slow/fast, sort each half, then merge two sorted lists — the standard linked-list merge sort.

approaches.title: Count 0/1/2 then rewrite values
approaches.explanation: Count each digit, then overwrite node values in order — the list becomes sorted without relinking.

approaches.title: Swap to the other head at the end
approaches.explanation: Each pointer walks its own list then the other's; they meet at the intersection because both cover the same total distance.

approaches.title: Reverse, add carry, reverse back
approaches.explanation: Reverse so the least significant digit is first, add 1 propagating the carry, then reverse back to restore order.

approaches.title: Add digit by digit with carry
approaches.explanation: Digits are stored least-significant-first, so walk both lists summing with a running carry and build the result list.

approaches.title: Unlink every matching node
approaches.explanation: Use a dummy head; whenever a node's value equals key, bridge prev.next past it and fix the successor's prev.

approaches.title: Head/tail two pointers
approaches.explanation: List is sorted; walk a forward and a backward pointer, counting pairs whose value sums to x.

approaches.title: Advance past equal neighbours
approaches.explanation: For a sorted DLL, repeatedly move next past nodes equal to the current value.

approaches.title: Reverse each block of K
approaches.explanation: Check K nodes remain, reverse that block, relink it into the previous tail, and continue from the block's new end.

approaches.title: Form a ring then cut at k
approaches.explanation: Compute the length, join tail to head to make a cycle, then advance (n - k) steps and break there as the new tail.

approaches.title: Merge the lists bottom-wise
approaches.explanation: Repeatedly merge each level's vertical sorted list into the accumulated result using the bottom pointer, keeping one flat sorted list.

approaches.title: Interleave copies, then split
approaches.explanation: Insert a copy after each original node, wire copy.random via the neighbour, then unweave the two lists.

approaches.title: Recurse over the digit suffix
approaches.explanation: Peel the last digit off recursively: atoi(s[0..n-1]) * 10 + lastDigit, stopping at a non-digit.

approaches.title: Divide-and-conquer power
approaches.explanation: x^n = (x^(n/2))^2, multiplying by one extra x when n is odd; handle negative n via 1/x^|n|.

approaches.title: Count = 4^a * 5^b with fast power
approaches.explanation: At odd positions only prime digits (4 choices) are allowed and at even positions any even digit (5 choices); multiply the two modular powers.

approaches.title: Sort the stack with recursion only
approaches.explanation: Pop all elements, then insert each back at its sorted position using a recursive insert that parks larger values temporarily.

approaches.title: Insert the bottom on unwind
approaches.explanation: Pop to the bottom, then on the way back insert each popped element at the stack's bottom recursively.

approaches.title: Append 0 always, 1 only after 0
approaches.explanation: Grow the string one bit at a time; place a 0 freely and a 1 only when the previous bit was 0, forbidding consecutive 1s.

approaches.title: Track open/close budgets
approaches.explanation: Add '(' while opens remain and ')' while closes exceed opens; emit when n pairs are used.

approaches.title: Take-or-skip each element
approaches.explanation: Standard power-set recursion: for each index branch on excluding and including the element.

approaches.title: Take-or-skip counted recursively
approaches.explanation: f(i, sum) = f(i+1, sum) + f(i+1, sum - a[i]) counting branches that reach exactly k at the end.

approaches.title: Any branch reaching the sum
approaches.explanation: Return true if either skipping or taking the current element eventually reaches sum 0.

approaches.title: Reuse the same index freely
approaches.explanation: At each step stay on the same candidate (reuse allowed) until the target is met, then move forward to avoid duplicate combinations.

approaches.title: Sort then skip duplicate picks per level
approaches.explanation: Each candidate is used at most once per branch; after returning, skip equal neighbours to avoid duplicate combinations.

approaches.title: Power set via take-or-skip
approaches.explanation: Recursively exclude and include each element, snapshotting the current subset at the leaves.

approaches.title: Sort then branch skipping duplicates
approaches.explanation: Include a value, then when skipping move past all its equal copies so no duplicate subset is produced.

approaches.title: Choose increasing digits to hit count/sum
approaches.explanation: Recurse over digits 1..9 keeping them strictly increasing, stopping at k digits; keep those summing to n.

approaches.title: Recurse over digit-to-letter maps
approaches.explanation: Map each phone digit to its letters and build every combination one position at a time.

approaches.title: Cut only at palindromic prefixes
approaches.explanation: From each start, extend the current part; recurse further only when that substring is a palindrome.

approaches.title: DFS with visited marking
approaches.explanation: From each matching cell, walk the four directions marking the cell as visited and restoring it on backtrack.

approaches.title: Place one queen per column
approaches.explanation: Fill column by column, checking the row and both diagonals; record the board when all n queens are placed.

approaches.title: DFS over open cells
approaches.explanation: Move down/right (classic rat-in-maze ordering) through cells equal to 1, marking the path and unmarking on backtrack.

approaches.title: Top-down memo on the start index
approaches.explanation: At each start index try every dictionary word that matches the prefix; memoize which starts can reach the end.

approaches.title: Assign colours vertex by vertex
approaches.explanation: Try each colour for the current vertex, accepting it only when no already-coloured neighbour shares it; recurse to the next vertex.

approaches.title: Fill empty cells with valid digits
approaches.explanation: Find the next empty cell, try 1..9 that respect row/column/3x3, and recurse; undo when a branch fails.

approaches.title: Split the string and insert operators
approaches.explanation: At each cut append a digit to the current operand or insert +, -, * (with correct precedence via a previous-term accumulator); keep expressions that evaluate to target.

approaches.title: AND with shifted 1
approaches.explanation: Shift 1 left by i positions and AND with n; a non-zero result means bit i is set.

approaches.title: Check the least-significant bit
approaches.explanation: A number is odd iff its last bit is 1; n & 1 isolates that bit.

approaches.title: n & (n-1) == 0 trick
approaches.explanation: A power of 2 has exactly one bit set; subtracting 1 flips all lower bits so n&(n-1) yields 0.

approaches.title: Brian Kernighan's bit-clearing loop
approaches.explanation: Each iteration of n &= (n-1) clears the lowest set bit; count iterations until n becomes 0.

approaches.title: Set rightmost unset via n|(n+1)
approaches.explanation: n+1 flips the rightmost unset bit to 1 (and clears trailing 1s); OR with n keeps original 1s and sets that bit.

approaches.title: XOR-based swap without temp
approaches.explanation: Three XOR assignments swap two integers: a^b^b=a and a^a^b=b.

approaches.title: Repeated doubling of divisor
approaches.explanation: Work with absolute values; find the largest power-of-2 multiple of divisor fitting in the remaining dividend, accumulate quotient via shifts.

approaches.title: Popcount of XOR
approaches.explanation: Bits that differ between start and goal show as 1 in start^goal; count them.

approaches.title: XOR every element
approaches.explanation: Duplicates cancel under XOR (a^a=0); the lone element remains.

approaches.title: Enumerate 2^n masks
approaches.explanation: For each mask 0..2^n-1, include element j if bit j of the mask is set.

approaches.title: XOR from 0 to n in O(1)
approaches.explanation: xorUp(n) follows a 4-case pattern on n%4; range [L,R] = xorUp(R) ^ xorUp(L-1).

approaches.title: XOR all, split by differing bit
approaches.explanation: XOR of entire array = a^b (two uniques). Pick any set bit to partition into two groups, each yielding one unique.

approaches.title: Divide out smallest factors
approaches.explanation: Try 2, then odd d from 3 up to sqrt(n); each time d divides n, record it and divide.

approaches.title: Collect divisors in sqrt pairs
approaches.explanation: For each i up to sqrt(n) that divides n, add both i and n/i; sort the result.

approaches.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes with prefix
approaches.explanation: Sieve primes up to R, build a prefix-count array, answer each query in O(1).

approaches.title: Factor map via trial division
approaches.explanation: Same as prime factors but returns a sorted map of prime→exponent.

approaches.title: Binary exponentiation
approaches.explanation: Square the base each step; multiply the result when the current bit of n is 1.

approaches.title: Fixed-size array with top pointer
approaches.explanation: Maintain an array and a top index; push increments top, push decrements, peek reads arr[top].

approaches.title: Circular array with front/rear
approaches.explanation: Use modular arithmetic for wrap-around; track front and rear indices plus a count.

approaches.title: Two queues, costly push
approaches.explanation: On push, drain q1 into q2, add new element to q1, then drain q2 back; this keeps the newest element at the front of q1.

approaches.title: Two stacks, costly dequeue
approaches.explanation: Push into s1; on dequeue, if s2 is empty transfer all from s1 to s2 (reversing order), then pop s2.

approaches.title: LinkedList as stack
approaches.explanation: Use a singly-linked list; push/pop at the head for O(1).

approaches.title: LinkedList with head/tail
approaches.explanation: Enqueue at tail, dequeue from head using a linked list with both pointers.

approaches.title: Stack-based bracket matching
approaches.explanation: Push opening brackets; on a closing bracket, check it matches the top of stack.

approaches.title: Store (val, currentMin) pairs
approaches.explanation: Each stack entry stores the pushed value AND the minimum up to that depth, so getMin is a simple peek.

approaches.title: Shunting-yard for infix→postfix
approaches.explanation: Scan left-to-right: operands go to output, operators pop higher/equal-precedence ops from the stack first.

approaches.title: Scan right-to-left with stack
approaches.explanation: Traverse the prefix string right-to-left; push operands, pop two and combine with parentheses when an operator is found.

approaches.title: Right-to-left scan, postfix combine
approaches.explanation: Traverse prefix right-to-left; for operators pop two operands and place operator at end (postfix form).

approaches.title: Left-to-right scan, prefix combine
approaches.explanation: Traverse postfix left-to-right; for operators pop two operands and place operator at front (prefix form).

approaches.title: Left-to-right with parenthesized combine
approaches.explanation: Traverse postfix left-to-right; pop two operands on operator and wrap in parentheses.

approaches.title: Modified shunting-yard for prefix
approaches.explanation: Reverse the infix (swap parens), apply postfix logic, then reverse the result.

approaches.title: Decreasing monotone stack
approaches.explanation: Traverse right-to-left, maintain a decreasing stack; the next greater for each element is the first larger value above it.

approaches.title: Monotone stack over 2n
approaches.explanation: Traverse the array twice (mod n) using a decreasing stack to find the next greater element in circular order.

approaches.title: Increasing monotone stack
approaches.explanation: Traverse right-to-left with an increasing stack; the next smaller is the first element smaller than current on top.

approaches.title: Count greater elements to right via stack
approaches.explanation: Use a monotone approach: for each element, pop all smaller elements and record the count of remaining stack size.

approaches.title: Left/right max two-pointer
approaches.explanation: Track leftMax and rightMax from both ends; water at each bar is min(leftMax, rightMax) - height.

approaches.title: Count subarrays where each element is min
approaches.explanation: For each element, find the distance to previous-less and next-less-or-equal via monotone stack; its contribution is a[i] * left * right.

approaches.title: Stack simulation of collisions
approaches.explanation: Push rightward asteroids; for each leftward one, pop smaller rightward ones until a larger blocks it or it explodes.

approaches.title: Stack contribution for max and min
approaches.explanation: Sum of ranges = sum of subarray maximums minus sum of subarray minimums; compute both via monotone stacks.

approaches.title: Greedy monotone stack removal
approaches.explanation: Build the smallest number by popping larger digits from the stack while k removals remain; trim trailing zeros.

approaches.title: Monotone stack for histogram
approaches.explanation: Use a sentinel-augmented increasing stack; at each pop the bar forms a rectangle spanning from prev-smaller to current index.

approaches.title: Largest rectangle per row as histogram
approaches.explanation: Build a histogram row by row (consecutive 1s height) and apply the stack-based largest-rectangle on each row.

approaches.title: Decreasing monotone deque
approaches.explanation: Maintain an index deque in decreasing value order; the front always holds the window maximum.

approaches.title: Stock span via monotone stack
approaches.explanation: Pop smaller-or-equal prices; span = current index minus the index of the first larger price (or i+1 if none).

approaches.title: Stack-based elimination
approaches.explanation: Push all candidates; pop pairs via knows() checks. The remaining candidate is verified in O(n).

approaches.title: HashMap + doubly-linked list
approaches.explanation: Doubly-linked list maintains access order; HashMap gives O(1) lookup. On get/put, move node to front; evict tail when over capacity.

approaches.title: Freq map + doubly-linked buckets
approaches.explanation: Track frequency with bucket doubly-linked lists ordered by time; evict from the lowest-frequency bucket's oldest node.

approaches.title: Sliding window with last-seen map
approaches.explanation: Expand right; if a duplicate is found, jump left past its previous occurrence. Track max window size.

approaches.title: Window with at most K zeros
approaches.explanation: Expand right; count zeros in window. Shrink left when zeros exceed K. Max window length is the answer.

approaches.title: Window with at most 2 fruit types
approaches.explanation: Standard at-most-K-distinct sliding window with a frequency map; shrink when types exceed 2.

approaches.title: Window sized by dominant char
approaches.explanation: Track max frequency in window; valid if windowLen - maxFreq <= k (replacements needed). Shrink left when invalid.

approaches.title: Prefix-sum count of subarrays equal to goal
approaches.explanation: Count prefixes with sum (total-goal); at each index the number of valid subarrays ending here equals how many earlier prefixes had that sum.

approaches.title: Sliding window with bitwise AND
approaches.explanation: Maintain a window where all elements are bitwise disjoint (used | nums[r] has no overlap); XOR out left elements until clear.

approaches.title: Complement counting with window
approaches.explanation: Count substrings NOT containing all three; subtract from total. Or: last positions of a,b,c; add min(lastA,lastB,lastC)+1 at each step.

approaches.title: Minimize window excluded from middle
approaches.explanation: Equivalently, find the minimum-sum subarray of length n-k in the circular array; answer = total - minWindow.

approaches.title: Window with at most K distinct
approaches.explanation: Expand right; maintain a frequency map. Shrink left while distinct count exceeds K. Track max window.

approaches.title: atMost(K) - atMost(K-1) distinct
approaches.explanation: Exactly K distinct = atMost(K) minus atMost(K-1); both computed via the standard sliding window.

approaches.title: Two-pointer with need/have maps
approaches.explanation: Expand right until all chars of t are satisfied, then contract left while still valid. Track minimum-length window.

approaches.title: Forward-backward window for subsequence
approaches.explanation: Find a forward match of t in s, then walk backward to shrink; record the minimum-length window and repeat.

approaches.title: Max-heap of size K
approaches.explanation: Maintain a max-heap of size k; for each new element, replace the top if smaller.

approaches.title: Array-based min-heap with sift
approaches.explanation: Standard binary-heap in an array: insert at end and sift-up; extract-min swaps root with last and sifts-down.

approaches.title: Verify heap property on array
approaches.explanation: For every index i, check that children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 are >= h[i].

approaches.title: Build max-heap from min-heap array
approaches.explanation: A min-heap array is a valid complete binary tree; just run heapify-down (max-variant) from n/2-1 to 0.

approaches.title: Min-heap of size K
approaches.explanation: Maintain a min-heap of size k; top is the k-th largest.

approaches.title: Min-heap sort for k-sorted array
approaches.explanation: Insert first k+1 elements into a min-heap; slide: extract-min into the output, then insert the next element.

approaches.title: Priority queue merge
approaches.explanation: Push heads of all k lists; pop-min, advance that list, push the next node. Builds the merged list.

approaches.title: Sort unique values, assign ranks
approaches.explanation: Collect distinct values in sorted order; rank = position in that order (1-indexed). Map back.

approaches.title: Sort by frequency, fill gaps
approaches.explanation: If the most-frequent task has count f, it creates f-1 gaps of size n between them. Answer = max(total, (f-1)*(n+1)+numMax).

approaches.title: TreeMap group by value, consume groups
approaches.explanation: Count each card value; greedily form groups of consecutive size groupSize using a sorted frequency map.

approaches.title: HashMap + merge with min-heap top 10
approaches.explanation: Store user→follows set and user→tweet-list. For getNewsFeed, merge tweets of self+followed using a min-heap of size 10.

approaches.title: Min-heap Huffman-style merge
approaches.explanation: Always merge the two smallest sticks; total cost accumulates the merged length.

approaches.title: Min-heap of size K for running kth largest
approaches.explanation: Keep the k largest elements in a min-heap; the root is the k-th largest at any point.

approaches.title: Max-heap seeded with (i,0) pairs
approaches.explanation: Push (A[i]+B[0], i, 0); each pop outputs one combination then pushes (i, j+1). Avoid duplicates via visited set.

approaches.title: Max-heap low + Min-heap high
approaches.explanation: Balance so sizes differ by at most 1; median is the top of the larger heap or average of both tops.

approaches.title: Bucket sort by frequency
approaches.explanation: Count frequencies, place into buckets indexed by count, then collect the top k from highest bucket downward.

approaches.title: Sort both, greedy match
approaches.explanation: Sort children and cookies; for each cookie (smallest first) satisfy the least-greedy child it can.

approaches.title: Sort by value/weight descending
approaches.explanation: Take items in decreasing value-per-weight ratio; fractionally take the last item that doesn't fully fit.

approaches.title: Give largest bill first
approaches.explanation: Track $5 and $10 bills; give change greedily ($10+$5 before 3x$5). Return false if change impossible.

approaches.title: Greedy with star backtracking
approaches.explanation: Match char-by-char; on '*', save positions and allow the star to consume extra chars on mismatch.

approaches.title: Sort by end time, greedy select
approaches.explanation: Sort meetings by finish time; take each meeting whose start is >= the last taken finish.

approaches.title: Track farthest reachable index
approaches.explanation: Maintain the farthest index reachable; if at any point i exceeds it, return false.

approaches.title: BFS-level greedy
approaches.explanation: Track current jump's range [i, curEnd]; when i exceeds curEnd, increment jumps and update to farthest reach.

approaches.title: Sort arrivals/departures, sweep
approaches.explanation: Sort arrival and departure times; sweep with two pointers tracking concurrent trains.

approaches.title: Sort by profit, fill latest slot
approaches.explanation: Sort jobs by profit descending; for each job, place it in the latest free slot <= its deadline.

approaches.title: Left-to-right then right-to-left
approaches.explanation: First pass ensures rising ratings get +1; second pass ensures falling ratings get +1; take max per child.

approaches.title: Sort by burst time, compute avg wait
approaches.explanation: SJF = shortest-job-first: sort by burst, accumulate weighted completion time.

approaches.title: Evict page used farthest in future
approaches.explanation: LRU simulation: on a page fault, evict the in-memory page whose next use is farthest (or never).

approaches.title: Sort by start, merge overlapping
approaches.explanation: Insert the new interval then merge all overlapping intervals in sorted order.

approaches.title: Sort by start, coalesce overlaps
approaches.explanation: Sort intervals by start; merge current into last result if overlapping, else append.

approaches.title: Sort by end, skip overlaps
approaches.explanation: Sort by end time; keep the interval with smallest end and remove all that overlap it; count removals.

approaches.title: One recursive walk collecting all three orders
approaches.explanation: A single DFS records the node at three moments — before the children for preorder, between them for inorder and after them for postorder.

approaches.title: Recursive preorder
approaches.explanation: The node is recorded before descending, then the left and right subtrees are visited in order — root-left-right.

approaches.title: Recursive inorder
approaches.explanation: Recurse into the left subtree, visit the node, then recurse into the right subtree — the classic left-root-right order.

approaches.title: Recursive postorder
approaches.explanation: Recurse into the left and right subtrees first and append the node afterwards, producing left-right-root order.

approaches.title: BFS level by level
approaches.explanation: The queue size at the start of each round is exactly the number of nodes on the current level, so the level can be drained into its own list.

approaches.title: Iterative preorder — push right first
approaches.explanation: A stack visit emits the node immediately; the right child is pushed before the left so the left subtree is processed first.

approaches.title: Iterative inorder with a left-chain stack
approaches.explanation: Push the full left chain, pop to visit a node, then move into its right subtree and repeat; the stack never holds more than one root-to-leaf path.

approaches.title: Two stacks — collect then reverse
approaches.explanation: The first stack emits root-right-left into the second stack, which reverses it into postorder order on the way out.

approaches.title: Better — reverse of a right-first preorder
approaches.explanation: Walks root-right-left with one stack (pushing left before right) and reverses the collected list; the reversed order is exactly postorder.

approaches.title: One stack with a last-visited pointer
approaches.explanation: A single stack holds the left spine; a node is only emitted when its right child is null or was just finished, tracked by a last-visited pointer.

approaches.title: Brute force — three separate traversals
approaches.explanation: Runs three independent recursive walks and fills one list each. Straightforward, but the tree is crossed three times instead of once.

approaches.title: Stack state machine — one traversal, three orders
approaches.explanation: Each stack entry carries a state: 1 adds to preorder and pushes the left child, 2 adds to inorder and pushes the right child, 3 finishes the node and pops it. Every node is processed exactly once.

approaches.title: Better — level-order BFS
approaches.explanation: Counts levels with a queue: every while iteration consumes exactly one level of the tree. Avoids recursion but needs O(N) queue space in the worst case.

approaches.title: Recursive depth
approaches.explanation: The depth of a node is one plus the deeper of its two subtrees. The recursion stack holds at most one root-to-leaf path.

approaches.title: Brute force — check imbalance then recurse
approaches.explanation: Verifies the height condition at every node and then recurses into the children, recomputing heights along the way. Correct but quadratic.

approaches.title: Height with a -1 imbalance sentinel
approaches.explanation: One recursive height function returns -1 the moment any subtree is unbalanced, so the walk stops early and each node is visited at most once.

approaches.title: Brute force — height at every node
approaches.explanation: Computes left and right heights for every node to find the longest path through it, then recurses. Heights are recomputed repeatedly, which is quadratic.

approaches.title: One-pass height with a running diameter
approaches.explanation: A single height recursion updates the best left-height + right-height seen at any node, so every node is visited exactly once.

approaches.title: Brute force — recompute gains at every node
approaches.explanation: For every node the best downward chains of both children are recomputed from scratch, so the same subtrees are walked again and again. Quadratic on skewed trees.

approaches.title: Single-pass gain recursion
approaches.explanation: One recursion returns the best downward gain of each subtree while updating the answer with paths that bend at the current node. Negative branches are floored at zero.

approaches.title: Brute force — serialize and compare
approaches.explanation: Both trees are serialized into preorder signatures with null markers and the strings are compared. Correct, but builds two full copies of the trees as text.

approaches.title: Parallel recursive comparison
approaches.explanation: Both trees are walked in lockstep: nodes must match in value and both children must match pairwise. Stops at the first difference.

approaches.title: Brute force — level order then reverse odd levels
approaches.explanation: Runs a plain left-to-right BFS and reverses every other level afterwards. Extra pass per level, but the easiest to reason about.

approaches.title: Indexed writes into a pre-sized level
approaches.explanation: Each level is pre-sized and nodes are written at either index i or size - 1 - i depending on the direction, so no reversal pass is needed.

approaches.title: Root + left boundary + leaves + reversed right boundary
approaches.explanation: The boundary is assembled in four parts: the root (once, unless it is a leaf), the left boundary top-down preferring left children, all leaves left to right, then the right boundary bottom-up.

approaches.title: Better — sort (distance, level, value) tuples
approaches.explanation: A DFS records one tuple per node and a single sort orders them by horizontal distance, then level, then value. Simple, but always pays the full sort instead of exploiting the BFS level order.

approaches.title: Nested maps with a heap per (distance, level)
approaches.explanation: BFS fills a TreeMap of distances whose values are TreeMaps of levels holding min-heaps, so each column is drained in the exact (level, value) order the problem requires.

approaches.title: BFS first write at each horizontal distance
approaches.explanation: Level-order BFS visits nodes from the top down, so the first node written for a horizontal distance is exactly the topmost one; a sorted map keeps the columns ordered.

approaches.title: BFS overwrite at each horizontal distance
approaches.explanation: Tracks the horizontal distance of every node in level order; later (deeper) nodes at the same distance overwrite earlier ones, and a sorted map yields the left-to-right bottom view.

approaches.title: Better — DFS visiting the visible side first
approaches.explanation: A depth-first walk that always descends into the visible side first records the first node reached at each depth. The right view visits right children first; the left view visits left children first.

approaches.title: BFS — first / last node per level
approaches.explanation: A level-order walk exposes the visible node of every level: the last node for the right view and the first node for the left view.

approaches.title: Better — iterative pair queue
approaches.explanation: Pushes mirrored pairs (outer children together, inner children together) into a queue and compares them two at a time. A null-tolerant queue is required because missing children are compared explicitly.

approaches.title: Mirror recursion
approaches.explanation: The left and right subtrees of the root are compared as mirror images: values must match and the outer/inner child pairs must mirror each other.

approaches.title: Brute force — search each leaf path
approaches.explanation: Collects every leaf and then re-searches the tree for the path to each one. Correct but repetitive, since the root path is rebuilt from scratch for every leaf.

approaches.title: Backtracking with path snapshots
approaches.explanation: A single depth-first walk keeps one mutable path; whenever a leaf is reached a copy of the path is stored and the last element is removed on the way back up.

approaches.title: Brute force — compare root paths
approaches.explanation: Extracts the root-to-node path for both targets and returns the last shared node. Simple to reason about, but it needs two extra path buffers.

approaches.title: Recursive search from both sides
approaches.explanation: The recursion reports the first found target upward from each subtree; the node where both sides return a hit is the LCA. Value ordering is not used, so this works for any binary tree.

approaches.title: Better — level min/max via DFS
approaches.explanation: A DFS assigns heap-style indices and records the first and last index seen on every level; the largest level span is the answer. Raw indices are never renormalized, so very deep trees can overflow.

approaches.title: BFS with normalized heap indices
approaches.explanation: Processes one level at a time, offsets every index by the leftmost index of that level to keep numbers small, and the level width is last index + 1. Long arithmetic prevents overflow.

approaches.title: Better — level-order check
approaches.explanation: Checks the property with a BFS queue instead of recursion: a node fails when its value differs from the sum of its existing children. Leaves are skipped.

approaches.title: Recursive property check
approaches.explanation: Each node compares its value against the sum of its existing children and then recurses; a leaf automatically satisfies the property. Uses only the recursion stack.

approaches.title: Brute force — distance from every node
approaches.explanation: Finds the root path of every node and of the target, then computes their distance from the shared prefix length. Each path search is O(N), making the whole walk quadratic.

approaches.title: Parent map + BFS from target
approaches.explanation: Parent pointers turn the tree into an undirected graph; a BFS from the target spreads one edge per level, and the queue snapshot at level k is the answer.

approaches.title: Better — parent map + BFS
approaches.explanation: First pass records the parent of every node; the second pass runs a multi-source BFS from the target over the left, right and parent edges, counting levels that actually reach new nodes.

approaches.title: Optimal — path walk + off-path depth
approaches.explanation: Extracts the only path from the target to the root; the fire reaches path node i after (depth - i) steps and then burns the deepest branch hanging off that node. The maximum of arrival + off-path depth is the burn time, with no parent map needed.

approaches.title: Brute force — full traversal count
approaches.explanation: Counts every node with a plain recursive traversal and ignores the completeness of the tree, so the O(log²N) guarantee of the optimal method is lost.

approaches.title: Perfect-subtree decomposition
approaches.explanation: Compares left and right heights: equal heights mean the subtree is perfect with 2^h - 1 nodes, otherwise recurse into both children. Only O(log N) levels are walked, each costing O(log N) height probes.

approaches.title: Why preorder + postorder is not enough
approaches.explanation: Inorder combined with preorder or postorder rebuilds a tree uniquely because inorder splits the subtrees; preorder with postorder cannot. The code returns two different trees that share the same preorder [1, 2] and postorder [2, 1].

approaches.title: Brute force — linear search for the root
approaches.explanation: Consumes preorder front to back and locates each root in the inorder window with a linear scan. Without the hashmap lookup every level of recursion costs O(N).

approaches.title: Hashmap of inorder positions
approaches.explanation: Inorder positions are stored in a hashmap, so the preorder root can be split into left and right ranges in O(1). Every node is created exactly once.

approaches.title: Brute force — linear search for the root
approaches.explanation: Recursively picks the root from the end of the postorder window and finds its position with a linear scan of the inorder window. The scan makes the worst case quadratic.

approaches.title: Hashmap of inorder positions
approaches.explanation: Inorder positions are precomputed in a hashmap so every root split is O(1); postorder is consumed right to left, which forces right-subtree-first construction.

approaches.title: Brute force — level-order codec
approaches.explanation: Serializes the tree breadth-first with '#' marking missing children and rebuilds it using a queue. Simple and robust, but trailing null markers make the payload larger than a preorder stream.

approaches.title: Preorder codec with null markers
approaches.explanation: Writes a preorder stream where '#' marks every null, which uniquely describes the shape; deserialization consumes the tokens front to back with a moving index.

approaches.title: Better — iterative stack preorder
approaches.explanation: Classic stack preorder: pop the current node into the result, then push right before left so the left child is processed first. Uses O(H) stack space.

approaches.title: Morris traversal — visit on first arrival
approaches.explanation: Same threading scheme as Morris inorder, but the node is recorded when the thread is created — the first time it is reached. Threads are still removed on the second visit, so the tree is restored.

approaches.title: Better — explicit stack inorder
approaches.explanation: Standard iterative inorder: push the entire left chain, pop to visit a node, then move to its right child. The explicit stack is what Morris traversal eliminates.

approaches.title: Morris traversal — temporary threads
approaches.explanation: The right pointer of the inorder predecessor is threaded back to the current node so the walk can return without a stack, and the thread is removed on the second visit. Inorder order is produced in O(1) extra space.

approaches.title: Brute force — preorder list then relink
approaches.explanation: Collects the preorder sequence of nodes, then rewires each node to its successor in that order with all left pointers nulled. The result is the required right-skewed list.

approaches.title: In-place flatten — Morris-style rewiring
approaches.explanation: For every node with a left child, the right subtree is attached below the rightmost node of the left subtree, then the left subtree moves to the right. No auxiliary structure is needed.

approaches.title: Brute force — search both branches
approaches.explanation: No BST ordering is used — every node is visited, so the tree is treated as a plain binary tree.

approaches.title: Guided walk — O(H) search
approaches.explanation: At each step compare with the current node and descend only one side; the search path is a root-to-node walk of height H.

approaches.title: Brute force — traverse everything
approaches.explanation: Full traversal that keeps the running minimum and maximum; works on any binary tree but visits all N nodes.

approaches.title: Extreme walk — leftmost and rightmost
approaches.explanation: The minimum of a BST is its leftmost node and the maximum is its rightmost — follow one chain of pointers.

approaches.title: Brute force — scan the whole tree
approaches.explanation: Visits every node and records the best floor and ceil candidates regardless of the BST property.

approaches.title: Lower and upper bound in one walk
approaches.explanation: One walk tracks both bounds: when the value is smaller than X it is a floor candidate, otherwise a ceil candidate; an exact match is both.

approaches.title: Brute force — scan the whole tree
approaches.explanation: Full traversal keeping the best value not exceeding X, without using BST ordering.

approaches.title: Guided walk — track best candidate
approaches.explanation: At each node: if it is <= X remember it and move right to look for something closer, otherwise move left.

approaches.title: Recursive insert
approaches.explanation: Recursive compare-and-descend; the new node is attached when a null child slot is reached.

approaches.title: Iterative insert — O(1) space
approaches.explanation: Iterative compare-and-descend with a loop; only one path of length H is visited and no call stack is used.

approaches.title: Recursive delete — successor replacement
approaches.explanation: Standard recursive delete: the 0/1 child cases reattach the single child, and the 2-children case copies the inorder successor (minimum of the right subtree) and deletes it from there.

approaches.title: Iterative delete — O(1) auxiliary space
approaches.explanation: Find the node and its parent first, copy the inorder successor, then splice the successor's child — no recursion, so the call stack is avoided entirely.

approaches.title: Inorder array — index the kth element
approaches.explanation: Inorder traversal of a BST is sorted, so the kth smallest is element k-1 and the kth largest is element N-k.

approaches.title: Iterative inorder — early stop at kth
approaches.explanation: Walk the tree iteratively and stop as soon as the kth node is popped; the largest side mirrors the same walk in reverse inorder.

approaches.title: Brute force — check every node against its subtrees
approaches.explanation: Each node is validated against every value in its two subtrees, making the check quadratic in the worst case.

approaches.title: Iterative inorder — values must strictly increase
approaches.explanation: A strictly increasing inorder sequence is exactly the BST condition; the walk uses an explicit stack and a long previous value.

approaches.title: Range propagation — long bounds
approaches.explanation: Every node is validated against an open interval; using long bounds avoids the Integer.MIN_VALUE/MAX_VALUE trap when node values equal those extremes.

approaches.title: Brute force — root-to-node paths
approaches.explanation: Build the root-to-p path and the root-to-q path, then the last common node is the LCA — works on any binary tree.

approaches.title: BST direction property — single walk
approaches.explanation: At each node: if both targets are smaller go left, if both are larger go right, otherwise the current node separates them and is the LCA.

approaches.title: Insert one by one
approaches.explanation: Insert the values one by one into an initially empty BST; each insert costs O(H), so a skewed input degrades to quadratic time.

approaches.title: Recursive bounds — upper limit per call
approaches.explanation: Preorder gives root, then left subtree, then right subtree; a running index and an upper bound decide when a subtree ends, giving a single O(N) pass.

approaches.title: Brute force — store the inorder traversal
approaches.explanation: Store the full inorder sequence; the successor is the first value greater than the key and the predecessor is the last value smaller.

approaches.title: Candidate tracking — walk down once
approaches.explanation: Walk down once while remembering the best candidate: go left whenever the current value is greater than the key (successor), right otherwise (predecessor).

approaches.title: Inorder arrays — merge sorted lists
approaches.explanation: Take the inorder sequence of both trees and merge them like merge sort.

approaches.title: Two iterators — merge in O(H1 + H2) space
approaches.explanation: Two stack-based iterators expose the next smallest value of each tree and are advanced like a merge, using only the height of both trees.

approaches.title: Inorder DFS — HashSet of seen values
approaches.explanation: DFS with a hash set — at every node check whether k - value was seen before; works on any tree.

approaches.title: Two BST iterators — two pointers in order
approaches.explanation: Forward and reverse iterators expose the smallest and largest remaining values; move the low pointer up or the high pointer down like two pointers on a sorted array, stopping when both meet on the same node.

approaches.title: Inorder traversal — collect and find inversions
approaches.explanation: Store the inorder nodes, find the first and the last inversion, and swap those two values back.

approaches.title: Constant tracking — first, middle, last
approaches.explanation: Track prev/first/middle/last during one inorder walk: a single inversion swaps first and middle, while two inversions swap first and last.

approaches.title: Brute force — validate every subtree
approaches.explanation: For every node check whether its subtree is a BST and take the largest size found; each check re-walks the subtree, hence O(N²).

approaches.title: Postorder DP — carry BST info upward
approaches.explanation: Postorder returns isBST/size/min/max for each subtree, so every node decides validity from its children's info in a single pass — a classic return-information-upward DP.

approaches.title: BFS over adjacency lists, count starts
approaches.explanation: Build the adjacency list, then every unvisited node starts a BFS that marks its whole component; the number of starts is the answer.

approaches.title: One adjacency list, then BFS and DFS orders
approaches.explanation: Build the graph once and show both traversals: BFS via a queue, DFS via recursion, from the same source.

approaches.title: Recursive DFS printing discovery order
approaches.explanation: Visit the start, record it, then recurse into every unvisited neighbor — the recursion stack is the DFS.

approaches.title: BFS over the adjacency matrix
approaches.explanation: isConnected[i][j] = 1 means a direct edge; every unvisited row starts a BFS that swallows its whole province.

approaches.title: Flood over 8-directional neighbors
approaches.explanation: Every 1 starts a component; the flood clears all ones connected to it, including diagonals.

approaches.title: Multi-source BFS, one layer per minute
approaches.explanation: All rotten cells enter the queue together; each BFS layer is one minute, and the count of fresh cells tells whether it ever finishes.

approaches.title: DFS recolor guarded by the old color
approaches.explanation: Remember the starting color; recolor each cell outside in, stopping at walls, borders and already-recolored cells.

approaches.title: BFS carrying the parent of each node
approaches.explanation: A visited neighbor that is not our own parent proves a cycle — in an undirected graph that edge closes a loop.

approaches.title: DFS with a parent check
approaches.explanation: Recurse from each unvisited node; if a neighbor is visited and is not the parent we came from, the graph has a cycle.

approaches.title: Multi-source BFS from every 1 at once
approaches.explanation: Seed the queue with all cells holding 1, keep -1 as 'unknown distance', and let BFS fill distances layer by layer.

approaches.title: Mark border-connected O's, then flip
approaches.explanation: Any O touching the border survives; mark all of those first, then everything left over is captured.

approaches.title: Flood from the border, count what remains
approaches.explanation: Land reachable from the edge can walk out; clear all of it, and the ones left behind are the enclaves.

approaches.title: BFS replacing one letter at a time
approaches.explanation: Every word is a node and a one-letter change is an edge; deleting words from the dictionary as you enqueue them keeps each visited once.

approaches.title: BFS by level + parent map — enumerate shortest paths
approaches.explanation: A level-aware BFS records every predecessor that reaches a word at its shortest distance. Backtracking from the target reconstructs all shortest ladders.

approaches.title: DFS sinking each island
approaches.explanation: Every unvisited land cell triggers a DFS that sinks the entire island to water, so it can never be counted twice.

approaches.title: Two-color painting with DFS
approaches.explanation: Paint every node 0 or 1; a neighbor that already carries our color proves the graph cannot be split in two.

approaches.title: Three-state DFS — visiting vs finished
approaches.explanation: State 1 means the node is on the current recursion stack; reaching it again means the edge closes a directed cycle.

approaches.title: Post-order DFS pushed onto a stack
approaches.explanation: A node finishes only after all its descendants, so pushing nodes when their DFS ends and popping gives a valid topological order.

approaches.title: Kahn's algorithm — peel zero indegrees
approaches.explanation: Start from nodes nothing points to; removing a node frees its neighbors, and anyone whose indegree hits zero joins the order.

approaches.title: Kahn's count exposes the cycle
approaches.explanation: If some nodes never reach indegree zero, they sit on a cycle — the processed count tells you instantly.

approaches.title: Prerequisites as a DAG — finish iff no cycle
approaches.explanation: Draw b → a for every prerequisite pair and run Kahn's algorithm; finishing every course means the graph is acyclic.

approaches.title: Record the Kahn order, empty on a cycle
approaches.explanation: The same peeling process yields the actual study order; if fewer than n courses come out, no valid order exists.

approaches.title: Reverse edges and peel from terminal nodes
approaches.explanation: Terminal nodes are safe; a node becomes safe once all its outgoing edges lead to safe nodes — peel them off the reversed graph.

approaches.title: First differing characters give the edges
approaches.explanation: For each adjacent word pair, the first mismatch orders two letters; a topological sort of these 26 letters spells the alphabet.

approaches.title: Plain BFS fills distances
approaches.explanation: With every edge of weight 1, BFS discovers nodes in non-decreasing distance so the first arrival is the shortest.

approaches.title: Topological order, then one relaxation pass
approaches.explanation: In a DAG every edge points forward in topological order, so a single sweep relaxes all distances without repeats.

approaches.title: Dijkstra with a priority queue
approaches.explanation: Always settle the closest unsettled node; stale entries with a bigger recorded distance are skipped.

approaches.title: Dijkstra without a priority queue — the O(V²) scan
approaches.explanation: Without a heap you rescan all nodes to find the next minimum each round; the priority queue turns exactly that step into O(log V).

approaches.title: BFS counting steps through open cells
approaches.explanation: Every move costs 1 on the grid, so BFS from the source reaches the destination in the fewest steps, avoiding walls and the border.

approaches.title: Dijkstra where the cost is the maximum jump
approaches.explanation: Keep the best achievable effort per cell; a move's effort is the max of the path so far and this step's height difference.

approaches.title: Layer-by-layer relaxation, one flight per stop
approaches.explanation: Relax all edges k+1 times, but keep the previous layer's distances intact so a path may use at most one extra flight per round.

approaches.title: Dijkstra, then the largest shortest distance
approaches.explanation: The signal reaches everyone at the slowest shortest path; if any node stays unreachable the answer is -1.

approaches.title: Count ways while Dijkstra tightens distances
approaches.explanation: A strictly shorter path resets the count to the predecessor's ways; an equal-length path adds them, all modulo 1e9+7.

approaches.title: BFS over the 0..99999 value space
approaches.explanation: Each multiplication is one step, so BFS over reachable products modulo 100000 finds the fewest operations; the first hit on end wins.

approaches.title: Relax every edge n-1 times, then probe once more
approaches.explanation: After n-1 relaxing rounds all shortest paths settle; one extra round that still improves distances proves a negative cycle.

approaches.title: All pairs through every intermediate k
approaches.explanation: Try every vertex as an intermediate stop; -1 entries become a big sentinel so unreachable stays unreachable.

approaches.title: Floyd-Warshall, then count reachable neighbors
approaches.explanation: Compute all-pairs distances, count how many cities sit within the threshold of each one, and prefer the largest index on ties.

approaches.title: Prim's — grow the tree with the lightest frontier edge
approaches.explanation: A priority queue holds edges leaving the tree; always take the cheapest edge to a node outside and add its weight.

approaches.title: Union-Find with path compression and rank
approaches.explanation: find flattens the path to the root; union attaches the smaller rank tree under the bigger one, keeping operations near constant.

approaches.title: Kruskal's — sort edges, union what is still apart
approaches.explanation: Process edges from cheapest to priciest; take one only when it links two different components, stopping after n-1 edges.

approaches.title: Components minus one after proving enough edges
approaches.explanation: Fewer than n-1 cables can never connect n machines; otherwise each union merges two groups and the answer is groups-1.

approaches.title: Union row and column ids, count the groups
approaches.explanation: Each stone glues its row and column together; within one group of size s you can remove s-1 stones, so answer = stones - groups.

approaches.title: Share an email, share a person
approaches.explanation: Whenever an email appears under another account, union the two accounts; then group emails by root and attach the owner name.

approaches.title: Add land, union with wet neighbors
approaches.explanation: Each operation plants one cell, raising the count by one, then every already-planted neighbor union merges two islands back into one.

approaches.title: Union existing islands, then test every flip
approaches.explanation: First union all adjacent land with size tracking; flipping a water cell merges up to four distinct neighboring islands, so try each cell.

approaches.title: Dijkstra where time is the worst cell on the path
approaches.explanation: Track the earliest time each cell becomes reachable — the max elevation along the path; a priority queue always expands the easiest frontier.

approaches.title: Tarjan's tin/low — the edge no cycle can bypass
approaches.explanation: An edge to a child is a bridge when the child's low value stays above our tin — nothing below climbs back to us or higher.

approaches.title: Articulation points — root child count and low checks
approaches.explanation: A node is critical when a child's low reaches at least its tin; the DFS root is special and needs two or more children.

approaches.title: Kosaraju — finish order, flip the graph, count
approaches.explanation: Take nodes in DFS finishing order, then flood the reversed graph from each unvisited one; every flood is exactly one SCC.

approaches.title: Memoized ways for the last one or two steps
approaches.explanation: The final step is reached either from n − 1 or n − 2, so the count is the sum of both — memoize each n once.

approaches.title: Tabulation — count ways for every step
approaches.explanation: Fill a table bottom-up — each step adds the previous two counts, seeded with ways[1] = 1 and ways[2] = 2.

approaches.title: Two rolling values — Fibonacci in disguise (space-optimized)
approaches.explanation: Only the previous two counts are ever needed, so two variables replace the whole table.

approaches.title: Memoized minimum energy from the last stone
approaches.explanation: Standing on stone i, the cheapest arrival is the better of coming from i − 1 or i − 2, plus the height gap paid.

approaches.title: Tabulation — energy for every stone
approaches.explanation: Walk the stones left to right and store the cheapest energy for each — from the previous stone or two stones back.

approaches.title: Rolling the last two stone costs (space-optimized)
approaches.explanation: Process stones left to right keeping only the costs of the previous two positions.

approaches.title: Memoized, trying all k previous stones
approaches.explanation: From stone i the frog may hop back to any of the previous k stones — take the cheapest jump and memoize the result.

approaches.title: Tabulated cost per stone with k-wide lookback
approaches.explanation: Fill dp left to right; dp[i] checks the previous k stones in one inner loop.

approaches.title: Memoized pick-or-skip over the last index
approaches.explanation: Either skip the last element or take it and jump two positions back — take whichever is larger.

approaches.title: Tabulation — best sum up to each index
approaches.explanation: Forward pass: best[i] is the better of skipping nums[i] or taking it plus best[i - 2].

approaches.title: Two rolling sums — skip or take (space-optimized)
approaches.explanation: Keep the best sums up to the previous two positions and extend with either decision.

approaches.title: Memoized loot ending at each house
approaches.explanation: Robbing house i forces skipping i − 1, so compare robbing it with skipping it and memoize.

approaches.title: Tabulation — loot up to each house
approaches.explanation: loot[i] is the best take from the first i houses — rob this one plus the plan two houses back, or skip it.

approaches.title: Two rolling values along the street (space-optimized)
approaches.explanation: Same recurrence as non-adjacent sums, sweeping the street once with two variables.

approaches.title: Memoized best points per day and last task
approaches.explanation: Recurse day by day, remembering the last task; memoize the best total for (day, last).

approaches.title: Tabulation — table of days by last task
approaches.explanation: dp[day][task] adds today's points to the best of yesterday's other two tasks; the answer is the best of the last day.

approaches.title: Space-optimized sweep over days and last task
approaches.explanation: Keep the best points per last task for the previous day; each new day tries every task except the one just done.

approaches.title: Memoized paths from each cell
approaches.explanation: paths(r, c) = paths(r - 1, c) + paths(r, c - 1), with the first row and column as the base case.

approaches.title: Tabulation — full grid of path counts
approaches.explanation: Seed the first row and column with ones, then every cell is the sum of its top and left neighbours.

approaches.title: One-dimensional grid DP (space-optimized)
approaches.explanation: Every cell is reached from above or from the left, so dp[j] = dp[j] + dp[j − 1] over a single row array.

approaches.title: Combinatorics — choose the down moves
approaches.explanation: A path is exactly m − 1 downs placed among m + n − 2 total moves — compute C(m + n − 2, m − 1) with rolling multiplication and division.

approaches.title: Memoized paths around obstacles
approaches.explanation: Same recursion as unique paths, but a cell holding an obstacle contributes zero ways.

approaches.title: Tabulation — grid with obstacle resets
approaches.explanation: Fill top-left to bottom-right; obstacle cells stay zero and block the paths behind them.

approaches.title: Row sweep with obstacle resets (space-optimized)
